choiceTexts: Sexual selection acting on a trait that improves mating success

answer.line: Selection against both extremes keeps the peak narrow and in place. That is stabilizing selection.

steps: Read the two clues: weights cluster tightly in the middle, and the average has barely moved.
Ask which shape gives a tight peak that stays put. Trim both tails and the spread narrows while the average holds.
Very small and very large babies both fared worse, so the middle wins. That is stabilizing selection.

choices.note: Directional selection moves the average one way over generations. The stem says the average held still.
Drift is random change in allele frequency, not selection at all. Chance would not hold a trait tight at one value.

choices.text: Sexual selection acting on a trait that improves mating success
choices.note: Sexual selection acts on traits that win mates. Birth weight is about infant survival, a different pressure.
Both tails trimmed, the middle favored: one narrow peak that stays put.
Disruptive selection favors both extremes over the middle and splits the peak in two, the opposite of one tight cluster.

lockIt: Peak narrows and stays: stabilizing. Peak slides: directional. Peak splits: disruptive.

playWith.label: Selection Modes tab: switch between stabilizing, directional and disruptive and compare the curves

panels.title: Stabilizing

visual.alt: Three small charts of birth weight, each with the starting bell curve dashed. Stabilizing, outlined as the answer, keeps the peak at about 7 pounds and makes it narrower; directional slides the peak to one side; disruptive splits it into two peaks.
visual.caption: Compare each solid curve with the dashed one. Only stabilizing keeps the peak where it was.
